title: OOP Face-Off: Java vs PHP in CodeIgniter
description: Compare how Java and PHP handle core OOP concepts, then see how PHP's OOP powers CodeIgniter 3.
congratsText: You can now read PHP OOP through a Java lens — and see exactly how CI3 builds on it!
objectives: Identify how Java and PHP declare classes and create objects.
Compare constructor syntax between Java and PHP.
Explain how access modifiers control visibility in both languages.
Compare inheritance syntax and keywords in Java and PHP.
Apply constructor and encapsulation rules to a CI3 model scenario.
Identify interface syntax differences between Java and PHP.
Explain how static members work in Java versus PHP.
Apply inheritance rules to CI3's CI_Controller pattern.
Explain how CI3 controllers and models use PHP OOP in practice.
recap: Java and PHP both declare classes with the class keyword, but PHP marks properties with $ instead of a type, and objects are built with new in both languages.
Java constructors share the class name; PHP constructors are always named __construct(), no matter what the class is called.
Both languages share public, private, and protected, but PHP quietly defaults an unmarked property to public.
Both use extends for inheritance; Java calls the parent with super(), PHP calls it with parent::__construct().
A CI3 model is a plain PHP class — it can have a private property and a __construct() that calls parent::__construct(), exactly like any other PHP subclass.
Java interfaces require full method signatures with types; PHP interfaces use the same implements keyword but let type declarations stay optional.
Static members belong to the class itself in both languages, but PHP reaches them with :: instead of Java's dot.
A CI3 controller's class Menu extends CI_Controller line and its parent::__construct() call are the exact same PHP inheritance pattern taught earlier — not framework magic.
CodeIgniter 3's controllers and models are ordinary PHP classes — everything covered here (classes, constructors, access modifiers, inheritance) is literally how CI3 is built.

chunks.text: Both Java and PHP define a blueprint with the class keyword — but PHP properties are marked with $ while Java uses a type declaration instead.

check.question: Which language requires a type before each property, like `String name;`?

chunks.text: Creating an object uses new ClassName() in both languages — the surface syntax looks almost identical.

check.question: Does PHP also use the `new` keyword to create objects?

chunks.text: The visible difference shows up inside methods: PHP writes $this->name everywhere, while Java just writes name or this.name.

check.question: In PHP, how do you refer to an object's own property inside a method?

quiz.question: Which line correctly declares a class property in PHP?

chunks.text: Java constructors are named exactly like their class — a Menu class has a Menu() constructor. PHP breaks that pattern entirely.

check.question: Does a PHP constructor share the class's own name?

chunks.text: PHP always names its constructor __construct(), no matter what the class itself is called.

check.question: What is the PHP constructor method always named?

chunks.text: Both constructors still run automatically the moment an object is created with new — that part hasn't changed.

check.question: Does the constructor run automatically when `new` is used?

quiz.question: Arrange the tokens to build a correct PHP constructor declaration.

chunks.text: Java and PHP share the same three visibility words: public, private, and protected.

check.question: Do PHP and Java use the same three access modifier keywords?

chunks.text: Leave a Java field unmarked and it becomes package-private. Leave a PHP property unmarked and PHP quietly makes it public.

check.question: What does PHP default an unmarked property to?

chunks.text: Getters and setters are just a convention in both languages — PHP doesn't force them, but hiding raw properties behind methods is still the safer habit.

check.question: Does PHP force you to write getters and setters?

quiz.question: Type the access modifier that means 'only this class and its subclasses can use this' — the same word in both Java and PHP.

chunks.text: Both languages use extends to build a subclass from a parent class — one keyword, two languages.

check.question: Which keyword builds a subclass in both Java and PHP?

chunks.text: To call the parent's constructor, Java uses super() while PHP uses parent::__construct().

check.question: What does PHP call instead of Java's `super()`?

chunks.text: PHP only lets a class extend one parent class, just like Java — no multiple class inheritance in either.

check.question: Can a PHP class extend more than one class at once?

quiz.question: Which line correctly calls a parent constructor from inside a PHP subclass?

sections.title: Constructors Meet a Real CI3 Model

chunks.text: A CI3 model class is just a normal PHP class — it can have its own constructor and private properties, same rules as any other PHP class.

check.question: Can a CI3 model define a private property?
options: No, models must be all public

chunks.text: Picture a Menu_model with a private $table property set inside its constructor — that constructor still has to be named one exact way.

check.question: What must that model's constructor be named?

chunks.text: Because $table is private, code outside the class can't touch it directly — it has to go through a method, exactly like encapsulation demands.

check.question: Can outside code read a private $table property directly?

quiz.question: Arrange the tokens to correctly declare and initialize a private $table property inside a CI3 model's constructor.

chunks.text: An interface lists method signatures with no bodies — a contract classes promise to follow, in both Java and PHP.

check.question: Does an interface contain full method bodies?

chunks.text: A class agrees to that contract with implements — the same keyword in both languages.

check.question: Which keyword connects a class to an interface?

chunks.text: Java forces you to declare parameter and return types in the interface. PHP lets you skip types entirely unless you choose to add them.

check.question: Does PHP require type declarations in an interface method?

quiz.question: Type the keyword a PHP class uses to promise it follows an interface's contract.

chunks.text: A static member belongs to the class itself, not to any one object — true in Java and PHP alike.

check.question: Does a static member belong to one specific object?
options: No, it belongs to the class
Yes, each object gets its own copy

chunks.text: Java reaches a static member with a dot, like MathUtil.PI. PHP reaches for the :: operator instead.

check.question: Which operator does PHP use to access a static member?

chunks.text: Calling a static method needs no new at all — you call it straight off the class name in both languages.

check.question: Do you need to create an object to call a static method?

quiz.question: Which line correctly calls a static method connect() on a PHP class named Database?

chunks.text: Every CI3 controller starts the same way: class Menu extends CI_Controller — that's inheritance in action, on day one of the framework.

check.question: Does a CI3 controller use the same extends keyword taught earlier?
options: No, CI3 has its own inheritance syntax

chunks.text: Inside that controller's constructor, the first line is usually parent::__construct(); — calling the parent class, same pattern as any PHP subclass.

check.question: What does that first line call?

chunks.text: Skip that parent call and CI3's core features, like $this->load, silently stop working — the parent constructor never ran to set them up.

check.question: What breaks if you skip calling the parent constructor?

quiz.question: This controller extends CI_Controller but never calls parent::__construct(). What's the most likely result?
options: The page loads but every model call fails instead
PHP throws a fatal syntax error on that line
The controller quietly falls back to a default view

chunks.text: Strip away the framework labels and a CI3 Controller or Model is just an ordinary PHP class — the same class/object rules from earlier apply.

check.question: Is a CI3 model just a regular PHP class underneath?
options: No, it's a special non-class structure

chunks.text: CI3's own base classes, like CI_Model, use the exact same static, private, and interface rules PHP already had — CodeIgniter didn't invent new OOP syntax.

check.question: Did CodeIgniter invent new OOP keywords for its base classes?
options: No, it reuses standard PHP OOP
Yes, CI3 has its own keyword set

chunks.text: That's the payoff: once you know PHP OOP, you already know how CI3 is built — CI_Model, CI_Controller, and every library are just classes and objects.

check.question: Does understanding PHP OOP help you understand CI3's internals?
options: No, CI3 is unrelated to OOP

quiz.question: Type the single PHP keyword that both a CI3 controller (extends CI_Controller) and a CI3 model (extends CI_Model) rely on to inherit their parent class's features.
